16.7.6 Reactivity of Alkynes

Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons like alkenes. Thus they resemble alkenes in most of their reactions. For example, alkyne add hydrogen, halogens and halogen acids much like the addition of these reagents to alkenes. However, unlike alkenes which add one molecules of these reagents, alkynes add two molecules in a step-wise manner. Characteristic reaction of alkyne are also electrophilic addition reactions.

It is to be noted that a carbon–carbon triple bond of alkynes, in general, is less reactive than a carbon–carbon double bond of alkenes, towards electrophilic reagents. This is due to the following reasons.

i. The triple bonded carbon atoms in alkynes are sp-hybridized while double bonded c-atoms in alkenes are sp²-hybridized. Greater the s character of an orbital, the more highly the electrons in that orbital are held by the nucleus. Thus, pi electrons in alkynes (50% s-character) are more strongly held by the carbon atom than in case of alkenes (33.33% s-character) and are less easily available for reactions with electrophile. This makes alkynes, less reactive than alkenes in electrophilic reactions.

ii. In alkynes, there are two pi bonds, the four lobes of which merge to form a single electron cloud. This cloud is cylindrically symmetrical about the inter-nuclear axis and occupies large volume (Figure 16.10). Thus, the pi electron–density per unit volume becomes low. Due to decrease in the electron density, pi electrons are not easily available to an electrophile and hence less reactive towards electrophilic addition reactions.

Terminal alkynes and acetylene are slightly acidic in nature. They readily donate proton to a strong base. Thus if acetylene or a terminal alkyne is treated with a solution of sodium amide (NaNH₂) in liquid ammonia, sodium acetylide or generally sodium alkynide is obtained.

Acetylene and other terminal alkynes are more acidic than alkanes and alkenes, as clear from pKa values given in Table 16.5. The acidity of an acetylenic hydrogen is due to sp-hybridization of triple bonded carbon atom. A sp-hybrid orbital has 50% s character in it and renders the carbon atom more electronegative than sp² and sp³-hybridized carbons. As a result, the sp-hybridized carbon atoms of a terminal alkyne pulls the electrons more strongly making the attached hydrogen atom slightly acidic.

16.7.5.2 Dehalogenation of Tetrahalides

When tetrahalides having two halogen atoms on each of the two adjacent carbons, are heated with zinc dust in alcohol, alkynes are formed.

16.7.6 Reactivity of Alkynes

Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons like alkenes. Thus they resemble alkenes in most of their reactions. For example, alkyne add hydrogen, halogens and halogen acids much like the addition of these reagents to alkenes. However, unlike alkenes which add one molecules of these reagents, alkynes add two molecules in a step-wise manner. Characteristic reaction of alkyne are also electrophilic addition reactions.

It is to be noted that a carbon–carbon triple bond of alkynes, in general, is less reactive than a carbon–carbon double bond of alkenes, towards electrophilic reagents. This is due to the following reasons.

i. The triple bonded carbon atoms in alkynes are sp-hybridized while double bonded c-atoms in alkenes are sp²-hybridized. Greater the s character of an orbital, the more highly the electrons in that orbital are held by the nucleus. Thus, pi electrons in alkynes (50% s-character) are more strongly held by the carbon atom than in case of alkenes (33.33% s-character) and are less easily available for reactions with electrophile. This makes alkynes, less reactive than alkenes in electrophilic reactions.

ii. In alkynes, there are two pi bonds, the four lobes of which merge to form a single electron cloud. This cloud is cylindrically symmetrical about the inter-nuclear axis and occupies large volume (Figure 16.10). Thus, the pi electron–density per unit volume becomes low. Due to decrease in the electron density, pi electrons are not easily available to an electrophile and hence less reactive towards electrophilic addition reactions.

Figure 16.10 Formation of cylidrical pi electronic cloud of triple bond.

16.7.7 Acidity of Terminal Alkynes

Alkynes in which the triple bond is at the end of the chain, are referred to as terminal or 1-alkynes. Some examples and general formula of terminal alkynes are given below.

Terminal alkynes and acetylene are slightly acidic in nature. They readily donate proton to a strong base. Thus if acetylene or a terminal alkyne is treated with a solution of sodium amide (NaNH₂) in liquid ammonia, sodium acetylide or generally sodium alkynide is obtained.

Acetylene and other terminal alkynes are more acidic than alkanes and alkenes, as clear from pKa values given in Table 16.5. The acidity of an acetylenic hydrogen is due to sp-hybridization of triple bonded carbon atom. A sp-hybrid orbital has 50% s character in it and renders the carbon atom more electronegative than sp² and sp³-hybridized carbons. As a result, the sp-hybridized carbon atoms of a terminal alkyne pulls the electrons more strongly making the attached hydrogen atom slightly acidic.
